title: Automating the seismic-resilient design of fiber-reinforced concrete using a physics-informed multi-agent system
abstract: Abstract The design of dynamically resilient concrete materials remains a complex, fragmented process that depends on iterative modelling, expert judgment, and poorly integrated workflows spanning structural analysis, material formulation, and seismic performance evaluation. To address this challenge, we develop an autonomous multi-agent system (MAS) that optimizes the life cycle design of fiber-reinforced concrete (FRC) for earthquake resilience. The system focuses on shear walls, beams, and columns that constitute the seismic load bearing envelope of multi-storey buildings. Rather than functioning as a general-purpose structural tool, the MAS is designed to intelligently generate FRC specifications, tailoring fiber type, geometry, and reinforcement ratios according to seismic inputs and project constraints that are automatically parsed by the system. The framework integrates agentic artificial intelligence (AgenAI) via an Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol with physical artificial intelligence (PhysAI) implemented through physics informed stochastic models for micromechanical prediction and energy dissipation damage analysis. A modified maximum entropy principle models fiber matrix interactions under heterogeneous uncertainty, enabling unbiased optimization of energy dissipative properties. In parallel, a CNN based computer vision pipeline employing a 3D U-Net architecture performs accurate segmentation and interpretation of micro-CT data. The architecture comprises five specialized AI agents built on Qwen-30B-A3B and Phi-4-14B large language models (LLMs), with context grounding provided by agentic retrieval augmented generation (ARAG) for domain specific decision making. Experimental validation shows that the system reduces human intensive design cycles by 75% relative to conventional finite element analysis workflows. It achieves 89.2% reasoning adherence, a mean predictive bias below 4% compared with stochastic simulations, and a failure state classification F1 score of 0.98. These results bridge micromechanical realism and automated, code compliant seismic design.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The growing demand for seismic resilience in structural systems has accelerated research into high performance, energy dissipating materials for civil engineering. Fiber reinforced concrete (FRC), particularly when enhanced with crumb rubber (CR) and various fiber types, has been shown to improve toughness, energy dissipation, and delayed crack propagation under cyclic loading. These properties make FRC a prime candidate for use in shear walls and other primary structural components in seismic zones (Atahan et al.,  5 ; Lv et al.,  18 ; Najim et al.,  20 ; Pan et al.,  23 ; Wang et al.,  26 ,  27 ; Wu et al.,  28 ; Zaitsev et al.,  31 ). However, these benefits entail trade offs in compressive strength and structural consistency. Researchers have attempted to resolve these drawbacks through careful mixture optimization and fiber reinforcement strategies (Lv et al.,  18 ; Najim et al.,  20 ; Pan et al.,  23 ; Zheng et al.,  33 ; González et al.,  13 ; Nonato Da Silva et al.,  21 ). Despite these advantages, the material design process for such composites remains largely empirical, requiring extensive laboratory testing and trial and error formulation. This challenge is compounded by the stochastic nature of composite microstructures, which conventional deterministic models fail to fully capture (Nonato Da Silva et al.,  21 ; Pan et al.,  23 ; Zhu et al.,  34 ).

Recent studies have shown that the seismic performance of FRC is largely governed by its cyclic energy dissipation capacity, hysteretic damping, and sensitivity to stress level under low cycle fatigue loading. These characteristics have been systematically examined through energy damage conversion models applied to steel, carbon, and basalt fiber recycled aggregate concrete (Cornejo et al.,  9 ; Wang et al.,  26 ,  27 ; Zaitsev et al.,  31 ; Zhang & Wang,  32 ; Zheng et al.,  33 ). In this context, Zaitsev et al. ( 31 ) combined scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and micro computed tomography (micro-CT) observations with a VUMAT based cyclic plasticity formulation to capture the low cycle hysteretic response of basalt fiber rubberized concrete. Their approach offers a physically consistent and computationally efficient representation of stiffness degradation and energy dissipation under seismic loading. The VUMAT (Vectorized User Material) concrete plasticity model is particularly advantageous for large scale shear wall simulations, because its vectorized implementation enables parallel computation and faster convergence compared to conventional UMAT or Concrete Damage Plasticity formulations. VUMAT leverages vectorized programming techniques that harness parallel processing capabilities on multicore CPUs, thereby reducing computation times. This consideration becomes critical when resolving numerous material points and cyclic load increments.

Recent developments in Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AgenAI) and Physical Artificial Intelligence (PhysAI), particularly when combined in multi-agent systems (MAS), have demonstrated strong potential to transform how material and structural design processes are automated and coordinated (Ascona et al.,  4 ; Farea et al.,  11 ; Henkes et al.,  15 ; Hu et al.,  16 ; Karniadakis et al.,  17 ; Martinez et al.,  19 ; Parisi et al.,  24 ). AgenAI emphasizes distributed reasoning, coordination, and task orchestration across specialized AI agents, whereas PhysAI focuses on embedding robust physics informed intelligence into computational frameworks, allowing systems to model, predict, and adapt based on the fundamental laws governing materials and structures (Farea et al.,  11 ; Karniadakis et al.,  17 ; Martinez et al.,  19 ; Xu & Liu,  29 ). PhysAI entails the fusion of physics based models with artificial intelligence to create autonomous systems whose reasoning is inseparable from the physical phenomena they simulate (Chen et al.,  8 ; Karniadakis et al.,  17 ; Martinez et al.,  19 ; Xu & Liu,  29 ). In the context of FRC seismic resilient material design, PhysAI is embodied in stochastic micromechanical models. These models leverage the maximum entropy principle to simulate fiber matrix interactions, crack initiation, and energy dissipation under seismic loading without introducing bias (Chen et al.,  7 ; Guan et al.,  14 ; Zhu et al.,  34 ). By coupling PhysAI with AgenAI, the proposed MAS unites physics informed micromechanical reasoning with intelligent multi-agent coordination, thereby creating a scalable, interpretable, and autonomous system capable of optimizing concrete formulations for dynamic resilience.

While the aforementioned studies underscore the valuable contributions of material and structural modelling, their applications have thus far been confined to specific functional domains. They have yet to incorporate advanced perception techniques such as micro-CT, or to leverage the generative reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and the orchestrated workflows of AgenAI. Our intelligent system addresses this gap by integrating MAS with physics informed models, micro-CT based perception, and context specific generative LLM reasoning. By coupling these elements with coordinated agentic workflows, we extend MAS beyond narrow functional simulations toward a holistic and intelligent framework for FRC material design, structural analysis, and lifecycle management.

Concurrently, the emergence of AgenAI, driven by LLMs enhanced through Agentic Retrieval Augmented Generation (ARAG), has introduced advanced capabilities for contextual reasoning and coordinated multi-agent workflows. Unlike conventional RAG, which performs static, query-based retrieval, ARAG operates as a dynamic, agent driven retrieval framework. In this framework, specialized agents autonomously trigger, refine, and exchange retrieved knowledge based on task specific requirements and intermediate reasoning states (Ehtesham et al.,  10 ; Singh et al.,  25 ; Yousefi et al.,  30 ). In the present work, ARAG enables agents to selectively access domain specific resources, including microstructural datasets, calibrated material models, and design constraints, and to iteratively integrate them into decision making loops. A key enabling concept within these systems is the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, an inter-agent communication architecture that facilitates autonomous coordination and task handover between specialized agents. Although still underutilized in civil engineering contexts, recent efforts have begun to explore this paradigm. Hu et al. ( 16 ) provided a consequential review of multi-agent reinforcement learning systems for collaborative construction engineering. These early implementations and theoretical works highlight the flexibility and modularity of agent communication, though they do not integrate domain specific modelling or microstructural interpretation (Henkes et al.,  15 ; Nowacka et al.,  22 ; Parisi et al.,  24 ). In the context of FRC design, the A2A protocol offers a scalable and interpretable framework for coordinating specialized AI agents, such as those responsible for parsing input parameters, performing predictive micromechanical modelling and homogenization, or interpreting image-based microstructure data, into a coherent and autonomous decision-making workflow.

To date, few studies have integrated high resolution microstructural analysis, AI driven material specification, and seismic performance evaluation into a unified, autonomous design workflow. The present work addresses this gap by introducing an adaptable multi-agent system that combines Agentic and Physical AI to enable real time, end to end optimization of FRC material design for seismic applications. The system parses project specific seismic inputs, models fiber matrix interactions using a modified maximum entropy principle, evaluates microstructural fidelity through CNN-based micro-CT segmentation, and coordinates material specification with downstream manufacturing constraints. The primary contribution of this research is the full cycle automation of FRC material and structural design within a single, coherent MAS architecture. Rather than proposing a new numerical solver in the classical sense, this work introduces a novel systemic concept for integrating physics informed, stochastic material modelling through modified maximum entropy modelling and energy dissipation phenomena into a unified, autonomous multi-agent workflow. This architecture bridges the gap between microstructural characterization, seismic structural performance assessment, and real time production-oriented decision making. By embedding ARAG enabled adaptive retrieval and physics consistent reasoning into agent interactions, the proposed framework transforms traditionally fragmented and iterative processes into a scalable, interpretable, and closed loop design pipeline, enabling reliable and real time optimization of resilient construction materials.

sections.heading: Operational logic
paragraphs: The proposed multi-agent system is a fully on premise, autonomous framework for the end-to-end design and optimization of fiber reinforced concrete under seismic loading. It constitutes a modular and intelligent framework designed to automate the design and micromechanical modelling of FRC materials, particularly those enhanced with rubber inclusions and optimized reinforcement schemes for dynamically resilient structural applications. Unlike conventional systems that rely on trial-and-error material formulation and static heuristics, the MAS dynamically configures concrete mixtures by combining fiber typology, reinforcement ratios, and material heterogeneity models. It simultaneously simulates probable cracking zones and damage distribution across structural components subjected to seismic loads. The primary objective is to assist material engineers and designers in generating tailored concrete compositions for shear walls, beams, and columns that form the structural shell of multi storey buildings in seismic zones (Fig.  1 ). Fig. 1 MAS workflow overview

At its core, the system identifies locations within structural members where increased fiber reinforcement is required to improve energy dissipation, ductility, and post cracking performance. It simultaneously recommends reductions or optimizations in steel reinforcement where fiber efficacy is sufficient. These decisions are informed by initial input parameters parsed by a dedicated Input Agent. Such parameters include building typology, number of storeys, seismic zone classification, and local construction practices. Based on these data, the MAS provides detailed feedback on likely zones of crack initiation and damage accumulation across structural elements under a range of simulated seismic scenarios. This predictive capability ensures that material formulations are not generalized but spatially optimized for specific regions within each element.

Rather than relying on computationally expensive finite element analysis (FEA) at this design stage, the MAS employs advanced stochastic modelling techniques to forecast failure by accounting for material cracking and energy dissipation behavior. Specifically, a modified maximum entropy principle (MEP) is applied within the system's Material Designer Agent to derive statistically unbiased property distributions for heterogeneous FRC microstructures. This approach supports probabilistic predictions of material behavior under dynamic loading while maintaining computational tractability. The MEP-based framework is informed by prior work on multi-phase composite micromechanics with inter particle, ITZ, aggregate, and fiber interaction effects. It enables robust simulation of the elastic and energy absorbing properties of fiber concrete without extensive empirical testing or costly numerical meshing (Chen et al.,  7 ; Guan et al.,  14 ; Nonato Da Silva et al.,  21 ; Zhu et al.,  34 ).

Within the proposed MAS workflow, the VUMAT-based constitutive framework serves as a unifying validation layer. It translates micromechanical predictions into structural scale hysteretic response across multiple FRC materials. The framework integrates carbon fiber reinforced concrete (CFRC) and basalt fiber reinforced concrete (BFRC) models based on energy conversion principles (Zaitsev et al.,  31 ; Zheng et al.,  33 ), alongside steel fiber reinforced concrete (SFRC) properties derived from González et al. ( 13 ). This integration enables consistent cross material simulation of cyclic behavior. The multi-material approach ensures that MAS predictions are benchmarked against diverse FRC responses, thereby improving robustness and minimizing model bias while maintaining compatibility with established constitutive formulations. Full scale structural modelling of the building load bearing shell, including meshing strategies, boundary conditions, and nonlinear cyclic loading, lies beyond the scope of this study. However, the MAS outputs validate material specifications and microstructural predictions that are directly exportable to external finite element environments. This export capability enables independent verification and seamless integration into existing structural analysis workflows, supporting comparative assessment and practical deployment across different fiber reinforcement strategies.

sections.heading: Agentic orchestration and functionality
paragraphs: The proposed multi-agent system addresses a persistent limitation in engineering workflows, where material design remains reliant on manual heuristics, fragmented coordination, and limited integration of micromechanical data and contextual AI reasoning. To overcome this limitation, the architecture integrates five specialized AI agents operating within adaptive, closed loop workflows that combine agent-based coordination with physics informed efficient stochastic finite element approximations. The system is deployed on a local workstation equipped with an RTX 4080 GPU, 64 GB RAM, and an Intel Core i9-14900HX processor. It utilizes Qwen-30B-A3B and Phi-4-14B large language models, context grounded via ARAG, as the reasoning backbone for interpreting seismic inputs, guiding optimization, and generating engineering specifications.

The functional capabilities of the system are distributed across distinct agentic roles, each engineered to manage a specific phase of the material design, characterization, and validation pipeline: A1: Input Parser Agent—This agent extracts seismic and project parameters, including soil conditions, seismic zone classifications, and building typologies, while ensuring compliance with relevant codes. It employs Qwen-30B-A3B, trained via ARAG on seismic codes (ACI Committee 318,  1 ; ASCE,  3 ; CEN,  6 ) and regional construction standards, to provide structured inputs for downstream agents. A2: Material Designer Agent—This agent implements entropy based stochastic micromechanics to generate statistically robust predictions of FRC performance. Using the maximum entropy principle, it derives unbiased property distributions for fiber matrix interactions and evaluates optimal fiber to steel reinforcement ratios. It leverages Qwen-30B-A3B for optimization reasoning and the VUMAT plasticity subroutine for cyclic energy dissipation modelling. A3: Microstructure Vision Agent—This agent analyses volumetric micro-CT datasets to characterize fiber orientation, dispersion, and rubber inclusions. A CNN based 3D U-Net architecture performs segmentation, while post processing routines quantify heterogeneity parameters. Results are passed back to the Material Designer Agent to refine probabilistic models. A4: Manufacturing Coordinator Agent—This agent translates optimized designs into fabrication ready specifications. Using Phi-4-14B and a rule based expert system, it generates material proportioning guidelines, reinforcement layouts, and manufacturing constraints compatible with local production environments. A5: Validation Agent—This agent verifies compliance and resilience of the proposed designs by cross checking against structural safety databases and performing lightweight simulations. It provides final approval for design export into external finite element software for full scale structural analysis.

An overview of agentic functionality is presented in Table  1 . Table 1 Agent functionality overview Agent Role Tools/techniques A1: Input Parser Agent Parses seismic and project data from engineers Qwen-30B-A3B (ARAG trained on seismic codes, standards) A2: Material Designer Agent Uses MEP-based stochastic micromechanics to optimize FRC composition and reinforcement Qwen-30B-A3B + VUMAT plasticity model + Maximum Entropy Optimization A3: Microstructure Vision Agent Segments micro-CT scans and evaluates inclusions CNN + 3D U-Net + micro-CT analysis A4: Manufacturing Coordinator Agent Translates optimized design into fabrication-ready specs Phi-4-14B + Rule-based expert system A5: Validation Agent Evaluates compliance and resilience Simulation models + Structural safety databases

To support this dynamic coordination, multi-agent orchestration is implemented using LangGraph, an extension of the LangChain framework designed for stateful, graph-based workflow execution. Unlike linear pipelines, LangGraph enables the definition of cyclic and conditional execution paths, allowing agents to iteratively refine outputs based on intermediate results and feedback loops. Each agent operates as a node within a directed computational graph, where state transitions are explicitly managed, enabling persistent context sharing and traceable decision-making. This architecture facilitates robust state management, allowing agents to maintain context across long running optimization tasks while integrating external engineering tools via RestAPI. The framework supports dynamic interaction with simulation engines, material databases, and document processing modules. Every agent operates as a dynamic, Docker based microservice architecture (MSA) containerized within Ollama, ensuring environment parity and isolated execution of LLM workloads.

For higher throughput or distributed deployments, this architecture is designed to be extended via vLLM and the Kafka ecosystem, enabling scalable, event driven coordination across heterogeneous computing nodes. To maintain the integrity of these complex cycles, Langfuse is integrated with the LangGraph workflow, serving as the observability layer. It provides granular execution traces to monitor inference latency and audit the fidelity of multi-agent reasoning against rigorous structural engineering benchmarks. This microservice oriented approach ensures that agent interactions remain modular, extensible, and robust under varying design workflow conditions.

The ARAG pipeline operationalizes domain grounded reasoning by enabling each agent to autonomously query ChromaDB for task specific engineering data, transforming the MAS into a situationally aware design environment. Specifically, A1 retrieves regional seismic codes and building standards (ACI Committee 318,  1 ; ASCE,  3 ; CEN,  6 ) to anchor project constraints, while A2 and A3 cross reference stochastic MEP models with micro-CT segmentation benchmarks to refine micromechanical property distributions. Simultaneously, A4 pulls real time fabrication constraints to generate production ready specifications, and A5 queries structural safety databases and established material models (ACI Committee 544,  2 ; fib,  12 ) to validate design resilience before FEA export. This role aware context injection ensures that every multi-agent transaction, from initial parsing to final validation, is a data grounded, traceable recommendation rather than a purely parametric approximation. An orchestration and workflow overview are presented in Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 Agentic orchestration and workflow

To maximize throughput across these high dimensional design cycles, the orchestration layer uses PyTorch native optimizations, including AWQ quantized kernels and vLLM managed speculative decoding, to accelerate LLM inference and vector retrieval in the ARAG pipeline. These performance enhancements are applied during Docker-based containerization of the Ollama microservices and are linked natively to Langfuse. This linkage creates a real time observability loop that audits latency against accuracy, ensuring that faster execution does not compromise the structural fidelity of agentic reasoning. By coupling micromechanical modelling with workflow orchestration, the MAS connects computational material design to engineering practice. The system generates optimized FRC configurations consistently and in real time. This integration reduces reliance on iterative calibration while preserving physical interpretability, supporting structural and material engineers in designing more resilient and resource efficient structures for seismically active regions.

sections.heading: Inter-agent communication
paragraphs: The functionality of the proposed MAS depends on seamless information exchange and decentralized coordination among its five specialized agents (A1 through A5). To achieve this, the system adapts the A2A protocol, an open standard communication framework, as the semantic and computational backbone. The base A2A protocol provides the transport layer via JSON RPC 2.0 and gRPC. Our implementation extends this standard by adding semantic interoperability, dynamic task orchestration, and distributed optimization logic tailored to structural engineering workflows. This extension ensures that outputs from one agent remain contextually interpretable and actionable for downstream agents within a physics informed design space. The adapted A2A protocol transforms the MAS from a linear automation pipeline into a decentralized, physics informed optimization framework that harmonizes symbolic reasoning, numerical micromechanical modelling, and imaging-based descriptors. By extending the protocol metadata schema to include structural ontologies, A2A integrates heterogeneous outputs ranging from LLM driven reasoning and homogenized constitutive tensors to micro-CT derived stochastic descriptors. All agents operate within a common representational domain. The protocol design supports resilience through distributed feedback loops, which prevent localized agent errors from propagating. Dynamic task delegation improves computational efficiency by triggering resource intensive analyses only when uncertainty thresholds are exceeded. The modularity of the A2A protocol also allows scalable expansion, accommodating new agents such as sustainability or lifecycle performance evaluators without systemic re architecture.

From an implementation standpoint, the A2A protocol serves as a lightweight yet robust communication layer that unifies heterogeneous AI agents under a common technical standard. It uses the JSON RPC 2.0 specification for structured message passing, enabling agents to exchange requests, responses, and error codes in a format that is both human readable and machine parseable. Secure inter-agent communication is ensured via gRPC channels protected with TLS, and every interaction is logged for auditability and reproducibility. The protocol supports advanced orchestration features, including message routing, task delegation with explicit return values, status broadcasting, and failure recovery using predefined fallback strategies. Each message is enriched with agent metadata that encodes task status, dependency trees, and contextual semantic tags derived from LLM parsing. This enrichment ensures that downstream agents operate with the necessary physical, semantic, and regulatory context. Together, these elements allow A2A to achieve high reliability, traceability, and semantic coherence across all levels of the MAS pipeline.

The interconnection with ARAG enriches A2A by linking physics grounded stochastic modelling with knowledge retrieval from seismic codes, regional construction standards, and experimental priors, thereby enhancing contextual adaptability and regulatory compliance. In this context, the A2A protocol functions as the nervous system of the MAS, enabling cohesive operation of specialized agents to deliver optimized, physics consistent, and constructible FRC material designs for seismic resilience.

Context injection into the LLM reasoning process is governed by a controlled orchestration pipeline implemented in LangGraph. This pipeline ensures that agent outputs remain strictly grounded in domain specific data. When the system receives a query or task request, the retriever subsystem applies a three-stage selection filter to optimize prompt information density. First, candidate documents are ranked by cosine similarity. Only those exceeding a 0.85 relevance threshold advance to the next stage. Second, a recency weighting algorithm prioritizes the most up to date records to maintain temporal accuracy in rapidly evolving project datasets. Third, all selected materials undergo normalization into a schema compliant JSON format to ensure compatibility with the MAS structured messaging conventions. Only after this filtration and normalization does the augmented context enter the LLM prompt template, guaranteeing that the resulting reasoning chain is both data grounded and audit traceable. Through its combination of standardized message encoding, secure communication, and semantically enriched metadata, the A2A protocol enables the MAS to function as a cohesive, distributed intelligence rather than a set of isolated components. This provides the technical backbone for integrating physics informed micromechanical predictions, ARAG based reasoning, and optimization workflows into a unified decision-making loop.

The A2A protocol is adapted around three core rationales: Semantic Interoperability—Engineering workflows involve heterogeneous data formats, including text-based seismic codes, numerical stochastic fields, voxelized micro-CT images, and manufacturing specifications. A2A harmonizes these formats by embedding structured ontologies and translation schemas, enabling each agent to interpret inputs without manual reformatting. Dynamic Delegation—A2A prevents the MAS from following a static, linear pipeline. Instead, it allows agents to trigger subroutines in other agents as required by the optimization loop. For example, A2 can request updated fiber orientation statistics from A3 when uncertainty thresholds are exceeded. Distributed Optimization and Robustness—The protocol ensures that decision making does not rely on a central bottleneck. Each agent exchanges uncertainty metrics and confidence scores with others, permitting redundant cross checks. For instance, A5 can challenge the optimization outputs of A2 if drift predictions exceed code prescribed limits. This distributed redundancy enhances system robustness, particularly under variable or incomplete data.

To mitigate the risks of information loss or semantic drift inherent in multi-agent communication, the adapted A2A protocol enforces a strict serialization schema using JSON LD and domain specific structural ontologies. This approach ensures that high dimensional data, such as homogenized constitutive tensors from A2 or voxelized fiber orientation distributions from A3, maintain physical consistency as they transition across specialized reasoning environments. Each message is augmented with contextual metadata, including uncertainty bounds, unit normalized variables, and provenance tags. This augmentation enables downstream agents to reconstruct the full decision context without ambiguity. Bidirectional verification loops, for example between A2 and A3, together with confidence aware message weighting, ensure that inconsistencies are detected and corrected early, preventing cumulative error propagation across the distributed optimization pipeline.

The protocol operates across three hierarchical layers. (1) Data Exchange Layer: This layer encodes raw outputs, including numerical tensors, probability distributions, and segmentation masks, into interoperable JSON LD structures with embedded metadata. (2) Semantic Layer: This layer uses domain ontologies for seismic, micromechanical, and manufacturing contexts to label variables. It ensures that a term such as "fiber volume fraction" parsed by A3 is unambiguously mapped to the corresponding stochastic descriptors in A2. (3) Optimization-Oriented Control Layer: This layer governs dynamic task delegation, consistency checks, and distributed optimization. Agents broadcast uncertainty indicators that can trigger re queries or refinement cycles. This layered design ensures that the MAS not only automates workflows but also enforces physics and context consistency across the agentic pipeline (Table  2 ).

sections.heading: Mathematical representation of the MAS operation
System architecture
paragraphs: The proposed MAS architecture is a multi-layered framework that unifies Agentic AI and Physical AI. Unlike conventional material design platforms, which are either rule-based (symbolic reasoning) or purely numerical (simulation driven), this architecture integrates both paradigms. AgenAI orchestrates workflow, communication, and contextual reasoning. PhysAI embeds physics informed models, stochastic micromechanics, and microstructural descriptors directly into the decision-making loop. This hybridization ensures that generated material specifications are simultaneously code compliant, constructible, and consistent with the physical laws governing seismic performance. For computationally heavy 3D reconstructions, such as volumes exceeding 1,700 slices from micro-CT scans, the system can scale to high performance computing (HPC) configurations with dual GPUs. Baseline MAS workflows, however, remain tractable on a local workstation. All agents run locally to preserve data privacy and autonomy, supported by a modular AI stack. The layered architecture is described below.

Data Exchange Layer: This layer normalizes heterogeneous data sources, including structured SQL databases, CSV datasets, and unstructured engineering documents, into a unified LangGraph compliant format. PostgreSQL, enhanced with the TimescaleDB extension, serves as the primary source of truth for project metadata, state management, and the ingestion of high-resolution microstructural descriptors and stochastic state vectors produced by A3. ChromaDB acts as a secondary search index providing persistent, vector-based memory for long term contextual awareness. By mapping document Universally Unique Identifiers (UUIDs) in PostgreSQL to high dimensional embeddings in ChromaDB, A1 can execute rapid relational joins on site specific constraints before triggering targeted semantic retrieval. The pgvector module further simplifies this infrastructure by storing high dimensional embeddings directly alongside relational records and A2A audit logs, creating a single pane of glass for project data. This consolidation facilitates the seamless integration of micromechanical weights and homogenized structural stiffness tensors. The hybrid integration ensures that intermediate results are propagated and retrieved efficiently, supporting a scalable orchestration in which additional agents or external simulation tools can be incorporated without disrupting the core execution logic.

User Interaction Layer: Users interact with the MAS via a REST API, which serves as the secure entry point for submitting FRC material design requirements together with seismic and project data. The API structures queries and design inputs and forwards them directly to A1, enabling seamless integration with existing digital engineering workflows.

Agentic AI Layer (Semantic Orchestration): This layer houses Qwen-30B-A3B and Phi-4-14B, deployed in Ollama containers running under WSL2 for GPU efficient local inference. Although Ollama serves the baseline local MAS, the architecture is vLLM ready to facilitate distributed HPC scaling across multiple GPU nodes. Orchestration is governed by LangGraph pipelines, which manage the stateful logic, cyclic execution paths, and task specific reasoning of the workflow. ARAG enriches the reasoning process by embedding domain specific knowledge, including seismic codes, regional construction standards, and prior experimental results. The dual database backbone of PostgreSQL and ChromaDB provides persistent relational and vector-based memory for long term contextual awareness. Through this integration, the Agentic layer ensures that parsed variables, code compliance checks, and optimization objectives remain semantically consistent, relationally valid, and dynamically updated across the MAS.

Physical AI Layer (Numerical Modelling): This layer embeds the physics of FRC through stochastic and constitutive modelling. Core components include: (1) MEP-based stochastic micromechanics to generate unbiased property distributions; (2) homogenization and VUMAT cyclic plasticity models to capture nonlinear hysteretic responses under seismic loading; (3) a 3D U-Net CNN (TensorRT optimized) for micro-CT segmentation, producing descriptors such as fiber orientation tensors, ITZ thickness fields, and void fractions. The outputs of this layer form the stochastic state vector ξ, which is ingested by the Material Designer Agent for entropy-based optimization. The core contribution of this layer is the computationally efficient linkage between a modified MEP and the stochastic micromechanical modelling of energy dissipation across the investigated FRC materials. The MAS does not treat AI as a simple parameter selector. Rather, it functions as a physics informed agentic workflow in which the A2A protocol, through the ARAG driven pipeline, carries ξ as a functional constraint. This bidirectional coupling ensures that every semantic decision made by the Agentic layer remains consistent with the FRC numerical and microstructural realities defined in Sects.  3  and  4 . The result is a robust system for seismically grounded design that neither a pure LLM nor a standalone numerical solver could achieve.

Communication Layer (Nervous System): All five agents (A1 through A5) are interconnected via the A2A protocol, built on JSON RPC 2.0 with gRPC and TLS encryption, semantic tags, and audit logging for reproducibility. Unlike the orchestration logic managed by LangGraph, this layer serves as the secure transport mechanism, governing the integrity of data packets exchanged between microservices. The layer governs task delegation, message routing, error recovery, and feedback correction, ensuring resilience and preventing the propagation of faulty results. The A2A protocol facilitates uncertainty exchange by embedding ξ within the communication payload, ensuring that contextual metadata and micromechanical descriptors, such as fiber volume fraction, remain physics consistent and automatically interpretable by downstream agents.

Validation and Feedback Layer: At the top of the loop, the Validation Agent (A5) evaluates whether MAS outputs meet seismic safety constraints, fragility thresholds, and constructability requirements. When violations occur, corrective feedback is transmitted back to the Material Designer Agent (A2), triggering adaptive re optimization cycles until feasible and resilient solutions are achieved. Table  3  provides an overview of the MAS system architecture layers. Table 3 MAS system architecture: technical overview and operation Component Technology/method Role in MAS workflow Integration in agentic–physical AI Data exchange layer PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB, pgvector, ChromaDB Normalizes heterogeneous data Bridges relational project state with semantic vector-based memory User interaction layer REST API (user input entry point) Accepts seismic/project data and forwards to A1 Provides secure human–system interface Agentic AI layer Qwen-30B-A3B, Phi-4-14B (Ollama/WSL2), vLLM-ready, LangGraph, ARAG Parses seismic inputs, interprets codes, orchestrates stateful logic Ensures semantic interoperability and scalable orchestration Physical AI layer MEP-based stochastic micromechanics, VUMAT plasticity, homogenization, 3D U-Net CNN (TensorRT) Predicts stiffness, crack initiation, energy dissipation; micro-CT descriptors Embeds physics-consistent models into optimization and design process Communication layer JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC/TLS, audit logging, semantic tags Manages data transport, interoperability, uncertainty exchange Harmonizes agent outputs into a single robust workflow Validation and feedback Lightweight simulations, code databases, uncertainty broadcasting Ensures compliance with seismic codes and resilience constraints Provides distributed redundancy and adaptive re-optimization Deployment environment Local workstation (RTX 4080, 64 GB RAM, i9-14900HX); optional dual-GPU HPC Executes MAS in cyber-secure local setting; scales for heavy reconstructions Balances high-velocity data accessibility with local scalability

This layered architecture achieves orchestration of heterogeneous workflows. ARAG enhanced reasoning provides contextual adaptability. PhysAI enforces material realism. The A2A protocol delivers resilient inter-agent coordination. Together, these elements enable the MAS to autonomously generate physics consistent FRC specifications that can be exported to external FEA solvers without manual intervention, all while maintaining cyber secure local execution. sections.heading: Multiscale representation of FRC
paragraphs: Within the MAS, fiber reinforced concrete is conceptualized as a three-dimensional hierarchical multiphase composite. In this representation, microscale heterogeneities and interactions, including fibers, ITZs, and voids, govern macroscale seismic performance. This conceptualization reflects the Physical AI paradigm, in which mathematico physical models, such as constitutive tensors, stochastic descriptors, energy dissipation laws, and homogenization operators, are embedded into the agentic workflow. This embedding enables autonomous yet physics informed decision-making. The Representative Volume Element (RVE) serves as the computational building block for FRC within the multiscale representation. Depending on user input, the Microstructure Vision Agent generates either cubic RVEs with periodic boundary conditions or cylindrical RVEs that capture inclusion dominated behavior. These RVEs are generated directly from micro-CT data (Fig.  4 ). Fig. 4 Computation of a FRC RVE:  a  cubic RVE with straight short carbon fibers ( D  = 0.6 mm;  V fr  = 0.3%) and crumb rubber ( D  = 1–2 mm;  V fr  = 10%);  b  cylindrical RVE with straight short basalt fibers ( D  = 0.6 mm;  V fr  = 0.3%) and crumb rubber ( D  = 15 µm;  V fr  = 10%), and  c  inclusions of the cylindrical RVE

The novelty lies in how these descriptors are not sampled by brute force but generated via entropy maximized distributions that incorporate only known constraints. The MAS agents autonomously integrate descriptors into the stochastic micromechanical framework, compute homogenized tensors, and return results to engineers.

sections.heading: Stochastic micromechanical modelling of FRC
Modified maximum entropy principle (MEP)
paragraphs: The stochastic framework of FRC requires a mathematically unbiased yet physically constrained description of material variability. To this end, the Modified Maximum Entropy Principle is employed within the MAS as the generative mechanism for constructing probability distributions of microstructural states. Unlike classical Monte Carlo simulations, which require prohibitively large samples, MEP ensures computational tractability while preserving the essential stochastic features of fiber, aggregate, ITZ, and void distributions.

The homogenized tensors are then passed to the Validation Agent, which integrates them with cyclic plasticity and energy dissipation models for structural level interpretation in shear walls, beams, and columns of the multi-storey shell. The outcome is a computationally efficient, physics informed framework that allows the MAS to bypass full scale stochastic finite element analysis while still accounting for heterogeneity and uncertainty. In this way, the MEP provides the mathematical backbone of the Physical AI component of the MAS, embedding constitutive physics and stochastic variability into an autonomous, real-time material design pipeline.

sections.heading: Interaction with fibers, aggregates, voids, and ITZ
Stochastic multi-storey shell modelling
paragraphs: To evaluate seismic performance effectively within the MAS loop, the homogenized microstructural outputs must be mapped into a reduced order MDOF model of the building shell. This transition from microscale uncertainty to macroscale performance is a multi-stage process that ensures physical consistency across scales.

sections.heading: Computer vision for micro-CT analysis
paragraphs: High-resolution micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) datasets provide volumetric information critical for capturing the multi-phase morphology of fiber reinforced concrete. The Microstructure Vision Agent automates the conversion of such volumetric data into structured descriptors by leveraging a 3D U-Net convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on paired micro-CT and CT slice datasets.

sections.heading: Neural network architecture and training
paragraphs: The Microstructure Vision Agent is built around a 3D U-Net CNN optimized for volumetric imaging tasks. The encoder decoder structure captures both global morphology and fine scale phase boundaries, with skip connections preserving spatial resolution during reconstruction. The architecture is trained on annotated micro-CT datasets using hybrid loss functions. This function combines voxel-wise cross-entropy, Dice similarity coefficients, and structural similarity indices to ensure balanced segmentation of inclusions across scales. Physics informed priors are embedded into the loss function by penalizing unrealistic geometries, such as disconnected fibers or over segmented ITZ shells, thus aligning predictions with micromechanical plausibility (Table  7 ). Table 7 The 3D U-Net CNN architecture logic Component Implementation in A3 Input 3D grayscale micro-CT volumes (voxel size 1–10 μm) Encoder Convolutional blocks with batch normalization + ReLU; down-sampling for multi-scale features Decoder Transposed convolutions with skip connections for phase boundary reconstruction Loss function Hybrid: cross-entropy + Dice loss + physics-informed penalty terms Output Phase probability maps (matrix, aggregates, fibers, ITZ, voids)

The CNN adopts an encoder decoder topology with four encoding and four decoding stages. Each stage comprises 3 × 3 × 3 convolutional kernels, batch normalization, and rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations. Down sampling uses 2 × 2 × 2 max pooling; the decoder applies transposed convolutions for symmetric up sampling. Skip connections convey spatially localized information from encoder to decoder, sharpening the delineation of fine structures such as ITZ shells and fiber tips.

Training runs on a dedicated high-performance workstation with dual NVIDIA A100 GPUs (80 GB HBM2e each) and 512 GB RAM. Batch sizes range from four to eight volumes of 256 3  voxels. The optimizer is Adam with an initial learning rate of 1e-4, decayed via cosine annealing and regularized by spatial dropout. The loss function combines three components: (a) cross entropy for voxel level classification accuracy; (b) Dice similarity coefficient for phase overlap maximization; (c) physics informed penalties that discard disconnected or physically implausible geometries.

After training, the CNN is compressed and accelerated with TensorRT to run efficiently on the local MAS PC. This setup keeps inference tractable within the MAS workflow while offloading training to dedicated HPC resources. Table  8  summarizes the architecture components. Table 8 The architecture component overview Component Specification Convolutional Kernel 3 × 3 × 3, applied at four encoding and decoding levels Layers 4 encoder + 4 decoder stages, skip connections between corresponding layers Training hardware Dual NVIDIA A100 GPUs (80 GB each), 512 GB RAM Training dataset Paired micro-CT grayscale slices + CT imaging layers of FRC samples Loss functions Cross-entropy + Dice + physics-informed penalties Optimizer Adam (lr = 1e − 4, cosine annealing scheduler) Validation metrics Voxel-wise accuracy, DSC, Hausdorff distance MAS deployment Optimized via TensorRT on RTX 4080 GPU workstation

sections.heading: CT image segmentation and bisection pipeline
paragraphs: The pipeline is not purely statistical; it is physics constrained. The ITZ thickness distributions are validated against gray scale gradients at inclusion matrix boundaries, and void shapes are parameterized by ellipsoidal harmonics rather than spherical approximations. Consequently, the extracted descriptors map directly onto the stochastic micromechanical modelling framework of Sect.  3.2 , reducing epistemic uncertainty and ensuring consistency with physical laws. The pipeline is summarized in Table  9 .

sections.heading: Dual-agent feedback loop
paragraphs: The extracted descriptors are communicated to the Material Designer Agent via the A2A protocol, where they form the stochastic state vector ξ following the Modified Maximum Entropy Principle. In this loop, the Microstructure Vision Agent delivers not only static measurements (fiber orientation tensors, ITZ thickness distributions, aggregate grading) but also attaches uncertainty metrics, including confidence maps from the CNN softmax layer and variance from ensemble predictions. These metrics determine whether additional scans or re segmentation are necessary. When descriptor reliability falls below predefined thresholds, the system dynamically triggers refinement.

sections.heading: Stochastic modelling results
paragraphs: Three reference FRC materials are considered: (a) basalt fiber-rubberized concrete (BFRC) based on Zaitsev et al. ( 31 ); (b) steel-fiber reinforced concrete (SFRC) from González et al. ( 13 ); and (c) short carbon-fiber reinforced concrete (CFRC) (Zheng et al.,  33 ). Material and geometric fiber parameters (fiber length, diameter, volume fraction, and geometry) are taken from those experimental studies and used as input design variables for the Material Designer Agent and for numerical calibration of the VUMAT model.

After stochastic micromechanical modelling, the material specific parameters for BFRC, SFRC, and CFRC are applied to macroscopic structural elements (beams, columns, and shear walls). Figure  6  presents the resulting total energy dissipation heatmaps for the three material types, highlighting distinct patterns of inelastic demand under seismic loading. Fig. 6 MAS predictions for structural element total energy dissipation: beam—a, d, g; column—b, e, h; shear wall—c, f, i

In beams, dissipation concentrates at mid span plastic hinges, reflecting flexural cracking and fiber bridging action. BFRC beams exhibit moderate dissipation, approximately 2,000 to 2,500 kJ, consistent with their relatively lower tensile strength and fiber pull out energy. SFRC beams, by contrast, show higher localized dissipation up to 2,500 to 2,800 kJ at the hinge regions. This results from the hooked steel fiber geometry, which provides anchorage and resists crack widening, and from the higher aspect ratio of steel fibers, which delays crack opening and increases hysteretic damping. CFRC beams display a more distributed dissipation in the range of 1,300 to 2,600 kJ due to the fine fiber dimensions and high tensile strength of carbon fibers. These properties improve crack control but offer less pull-out toughness compared to steel (Fig.  6 ).

Columns concentrate dissipation at the base and, under higher moment reversals, near the top, highlighting the critical role of flexural axial interaction. BFRC columns dissipate 700 to 2,100 kJ, concentrated sharply at the base, suggesting vulnerability to brittle cracking once the energy threshold is exceeded. SFRC columns reach higher cumulative dissipation up to 2,500 to 2,750 kJ with broader spread along the lower half of the column, reflecting greater resilience and reduced residual drift due to enhanced crack bridging capacity. CFRC columns exhibit intermediate levels of 1,600 to 2,450 kJ with a more gradual decay along the height, indicating beneficial stiffness recovery but less ductile energy absorption than SFRC (Fig.  6 ).

Finally, shear walls exhibit diagonal banding in dissipation fields, consistent with shear flexural interaction under cyclic lateral loads. BFRC shear walls display concentrated dissipation near the wall base, while SFRC walls show a broader diagonal distribution, reflecting higher crack resistance and cumulative energy absorption capacity. CFRC walls provide improved peak strength but slightly reduced total energy absorption compared to SFRC, consistent with the MAS stochastic predictions and literature evidence. SFRC walls demonstrate the highest dissipation, approximately 2,670 to 2,950 kJ, distributed diagonally, consistent with experimental findings that hooked steel fibers enhance energy absorption and limit damage concentration. The acquired prediction trend overview is demonstrated in Table  12 . sections.heading: System validation
paragraphs: This subsection validates the MAS across four hierarchical levels: (i) ARAG pipeline performance; (ii) microstructure segmentation accuracy of the Microstructure Vision Agent; (iii) material level predictive fidelity of deterministic and stochastic micromechanics; and (iv) structural level performance in terms of classification and fragility. By combining agentic orchestration, stochastic modelling, and physics informed approaches, the MAS provides a bridge between experimental characterization and predictive seismic performance.

sections.heading: ARAG performance validation and observability
paragraphs: The ARAG enhanced MAS was evaluated on a dataset of 3,000 simulated seismic design and material optimization scenarios accumulated over three years. The dataset comprises parametrically generated building cases that combine variations in seismic hazard intensity (PGA from 0.15 g to 0.45 g), soil classes, structural typologies (frame shear wall systems), and performance targets (drift limits, ductility demands), together with stochastic variations in FRC composition (fiber type, volume fraction, aspect ratio, rubber content). The MAS generated these scenarios within its MEP based micromechanical workflow, ensuring statistically representative coverage of both structural demand and material uncertainty spaces. The ARAG pipeline dynamically switches between two execution pathways: (i) a rapid inference mode, where precomputed or database-retrieved microstructural descriptors enable end-to-end design generation within seconds, and (ii) a high-fidelity reconstruction mode, where raw micro-CT data triggers full 3D segmentation and micromechanical re-evaluation, extending total workflow execution time to ~ 20–25 min while providing significantly higher material realism and model fidelity.

Benchmarking showed an average semantic retrieval latency of 530 ms per agent query, with a top 30 context relevance hit rate of 92.3%. Although retrieval of high dimensional context remains sub second, the system distinguishes between inference only and generative workflows based on the availability of microstructural data. When the ARAG pipeline identifies a context hit within the Micro-CT Benchmarks DB, the system bypasses the primary segmentation stack, reducing the total design cycle time from approximately 24 min to under 155 s. Conversely, for novel fiber reinforced compositions that require de novo characterization, the end-to-end workflow latency is dominated by the Microstructure Vision Agent, which takes a median of 22 min for a 1,700 slice volumetric reconstruction on a local RTX 4080 workstation. Reasoning accuracy, cross validated against verified seismic design workflows, reached 89.2%, confirming that the MAS effectively navigates these two paths without sacrificing technical fidelity (Table  13 ). Table 13 ARAG performance Metric Measured value Evaluation method Retrieval latency 530 ms (avg per agent call) Direct instrumentation of the A2A Gateway across 5,000 cycles Cached cycle time 155 s Standard execution when Micro-CT data is pre-indexed Discovery cycle time  ~ 22 min Execution including 3D U-Net and MEP convergence Context relevance 92.3% (top-30 hit) Manual review of retrieved material specs by senior engineers Reasoning accuracy 89.2% (adherence) Cross-validation against archived seismic design workflows

These results were enabled by the native integration of Langfuse, which provided the observability necessary to fine tune the multi-agent orchestration. Step by step execution tracing allowed us to identify and eliminate latency bottlenecks in the A2A protocol schema normalization stage, ensuring stable throughput even under high concurrency loads. The 89.2% reasoning adherence was further validated using an automated evaluator suite that scored the alignment between MAS generated decision paths and the ground truth logic of historical engineering approvals. Empirical traces confirmed that role aware context filtering reduced cross agent retrieval time by up to 55%, significantly accelerating the generation of executive grade design specifications without sacrificing technical fidelity.

To address epistemic uncertainty explicitly, the ARAG pipeline incorporates uncertainty aware context retrieval and validation mechanisms. Each agent propagates confidence scores and stochastic bounds associated with the MEP derived state vector. Scenarios with elevated uncertainty or low context relevance scores automatically trigger the high-fidelity reconstruction pathway and, when necessary, downstream FEA based validation through the Validation Agent. This ensures that surrogate predictions are not accepted outside their domain of reliability. To further verify system generalization and engineering utility, 14 independent structural engineers audited the MAS workflow, yielding a Peer Validation Adherence (PVA) score of 91.4%. This metric quantifies the normalized similarity index between MAS generated design vectors and independent ground truth benchmarks developed by the experts through parallel manual FEA simulations and code compliance assessments. The engineers documented their validations via standardized performance matrices, which evaluated the convergence of agentic reasoning with established structural benchmarks for hysteretic energy dissipation, fiber anchorage efficiency, and ductility limits across 120 distinct seismic loading scenarios.

sections.heading: Microstructure segmentation validation
paragraphs: A 3D U-Net architecture serves as the backbone of the CNN based computer vision pipeline. The model was trained on a curated dataset of 196 volumetric micro-CT scans (resolution 512 × 512 × 1,700 voxels) encompassing BFRC, SFRC, and CFRC specimens. Voxel wise annotations were generated through a semi-automated workflow that combines threshold-based segmentation with expert manual refinement. The dataset was split into training, validation, and test subsets using a 70/15/15 ratio at the volume level to prevent spatial leakage. Class imbalance posed a challenge: fiber voxels constitute less than 2% of the total volume. To mitigate this, we used a weighted Dice loss and targeted patch-based sampling. Training was performed on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU with mixed precision optimization. After training, we enhanced inference efficiency through model graph optimization and kernel fusion using TensorRT and PyTorch JIT compilation, which reduced memory footprint and accelerated inference. The optimized model was then deployed on a local RTX 4080 GPU and scaled to a dual GPU HPC environment for large volume reconstruction, ensuring consistent performance across varying computational setups.

The A3 achieves high fidelity across all material systems, with Dice coefficients reaching 0.94 for aggregates and 0.87 to 0.89 for fibers. Fibers remain the most challenging phase to segment, exhibiting slightly higher Hausdorff distances (approximately 0.28 mm to 0.32 mm) due to their slender morphology and blurred voxel boundaries in micro-CT data. The primary sources of error include voxel resolution limits (fiber diameters approaching voxel size), grayscale overlap between the ITZ and matrix, and severe class imbalance (fiber voxels below 2%). These factors lead to localized misclassifications that, while volumetrically small, influence downstream micromechanical modelling. As shown in Table  14 , segmentation performance remains consistent across BFRC, CFRC, and SFRC. Inter material variation in Dice coefficients stays within ± 0.02 across all phases, IoU deviations within ± 0.03, and Hausdorff distance variations within ± 0.04 mm. These narrow bounds indicate that segmentation accuracy is largely invariant to fiber typology, confirming the robustness and generalizability of the 3D U-Net based vision pipeline across heterogeneous FRC microstructures. Traditional CNN segmentation operates solely on pixel or voxel intensity. In contrast, physics informed LLMs could condition segmentation on expected morphology, including fiber aspect ratio, ITZ thickness distributions, and void size statistics, thereby embedding constitutive priors directly into the segmentation process. Large Concept Models (LCMs) go further by incorporating domain level rules of fracture mechanics and composite behavior, enabling segmentation not merely by appearance but by structural role. Such models would reduce fiber matrix misclassification, accelerate segmentation beyond the current median of 22 min per stack, and usher in a new generation of Physical AI where perception is constrained and guided by mechanics.

sections.heading: Material-level predictive accuracy
paragraphs: To ensure generality beyond a single material system, we evaluated the deterministic and stochastic micromechanical models across BFRC, CFRC, and SFRC materials. The results show that the relative performance trends observed for BFRC are consistently preserved across CFRC and SFRC. Specifically, the Mori–Tanaka approach systematically overestimates energy dissipation by approximately 8.5% to 10.2%, whereas the MEP posterior reduces this bias to within 1.8% to 2.8% across all materials. Similarly, RMSE values for the MEP posterior remain within 2% to 5% of experimental means, compared to 8% to 10% for the deterministic model. This limitation arises because the Mori–Tanaka model assumes uniform strain distributions and linear homogenization, which prevents it from accounting for key phenomena central to energy dissipation in FRC, such as cyclic plasticity, crack bridging, and hysteresis. Even when modified with VUMAT compatible softening laws for this study, its predictive capabilities remained narrow and conservative. These deviations indicate that inter material variation in predictive accuracy stays within ± 1% for bias and within ± 15% for RMSE relative differences, confirming the robustness of the stochastic framework across distinct fiber typologies. Comparison of deterministic (Mori–Tanaka) and stochastic (MEP posterior) model is demonstrated in Table  15 . sections.heading: Structural-level validation
paragraphs: Structural-level finite element validation was performed in ABAQUS under low-cycle, earthquake-representative loading conditions, using quasi-static cyclic displacement protocols at a strain rate of 10⁻ 2  s⁻ 1  and stress demands ranging from 18 to 28 MPa in critical hinge regions—typical of RC elements subjected to moderate-to-severe seismic drifts (Fig.  7 ). Beam and column geometries followed standard mid-rise residential dimensions (rectangular RC beams and columns), while the shear wall configuration was adopted from Zaitsev et al. ( 31 ). To ensure system independence and robustness, we benchmarked the MAS predictions against three distinct energy dissipation numerical frameworks integrated into the VUMAT model for FEA in Abaqus (Wang et al.,  26 ,  27 ; Zaitsev et al.,  31 ; Zheng et al.,  33 ). Across all datasets, the MAS prediction maintains a monotonic increase with drift and accurately preserves the physically consistent spacing among materials: SFRC > BFRC > CFRC. Steel fibers possess high ductility and superior bond slip characteristics, leading to extensive hysteretic energy dissipation through fiber pull out and plastic deformation. Basalt fibers offer a balance with high elongation at break, providing significant dissipation through distributed micro cracking and fiber matrix debonding. Carbon fibers, while high in stiffness and relatively brittle, provide exceptional strength. Their total energy dissipation is lower because the primary failure mode, namely fiber fracture or abrupt debonding, involves less hysteretic work than the gradual pull out seen in steel or basalt. Fig. 7 Structure-level validation for total energy dissipation VS Drift:  a  beam,  b  column, and  c  shear wall

The curves from Zheng et al. ( 33 ) consistently exhibited slightly higher dissipation values due to their energy conversion-based damage modelling, which captures enhanced hysteretic damping under high cyclic demand. Conversely, the curves from Wang et al., ( 26 ,  27 ) were generally more conservative, using simplified hysteresis assumptions that led to lower total energy dissipation estimates. The observed results highlight a significant divergence in energy dissipation estimates for high stiffness materials. CFRC demonstrates wider sensitivity to the chosen numerical philosophy, specifically between energy conversion and hysteretic damping frameworks, compared to BFRC. This modelling spread underscores the inherent complexity of simulating nonlinear behavior in brittle composites under cyclic seismic demand. Notably, the MAS prediction consistently tracks the median of this performance envelope across all materials, signifying high systemic stability and robust resistance to model specific bias.

Across structural elements, MAS derived dissipation trends closely matched ABAQUS VUMAT simulations, with mean bias values remaining below 4% for all fiber reinforced concrete types (BFRC, SFRC, CFRC). RMSE values were similarly low, typically 50–80 kJ relative to dissipation magnitudes of 1.5–3.0 MJ, indicating minimal pointwise deviation and stable convergence of the MAS micromechanical predictions toward the underlying cyclic plasticity model. For beams, the mean bias ranged from 0.89 to 2.89%, with corresponding RMSE values of 50–66 kJ, indicating excellent agreement in flexural hinge energy dissipation. For columns, the MAS achieved mean bias values of 0.55%–3.78% and RMSE levels of 66–79 kJ, reflecting robust fidelity under combined axial flexural cyclic demand. For shear walls, mean bias values of 1.18% to 3.33% and RMSE values near 50 kJ confirm the capability of the MAS to accurately reproduce diagonal shear flexural interaction and base plasticity energy dissipation trends. Given that total energy dissipation magnitudes fall in the range of 1.5–3.0 MJ, these RMSE values represent only 2%–5% relative error, demonstrating tight pointwise agreement and stable convergence of the MAS micromechanical and MEP predictions toward the calibrated VUMAT cyclic plasticity model. Collectively, the results confirm that the homogenization pipeline and structural estimators of the MAS accurately recover material dependent hysteretic energy dissipation across all drift levels and element types.

The MAS achieves accurate classification of structural failure states, with overall precision and recall of approximately 0.98. Columns and beams reach near perfect performance, while shear walls lag slightly with an F1 score of 0.976, reflecting the greater complexity of shear dominated damage. The MAS operation is conveyed by confusion matrix (Fig.  8 ) and by the system classification performance metrics (Fig.  9 ). Fig. 8 Confusion matrix for structural classification (failure versus safe) Fig. 9 MAS classification performance metrics per structural element

To evaluate the contribution of individual system components and hardware efficiency, we conducted a targeted ablation study. We compared the end-to-end performance of the full MAS against a baseline vision agnostic pipeline. The integration of the Microstructure Vision Agent improved material level predictive accuracy by 12% relative to manual data entry of fiber parameters. Computational scalability tests showed that transitioning from a single GPU consumer grade setup to a dual GPU configuration reduced volumetric reconstruction times by 28%, while maintaining identical reasoning adherence. These results indicate that although the MAS logic is hardware agnostic, the vision intensive segments of the ARAG pipeline scale linearly with local compute resources. We also performed architectural ablation to compare the current parallel (swarm) agentic architecture against an initial hierarchical framework in which the Material Designer Agent served as a central governor for agents A1, A3, A4, and A5. The hierarchical model provided a rigid chain of command but introduced significant latency bottlenecks and inhibited the asynchronous processing required for the Microstructure Vision Agent. The transition to a parallel architecture was adopted to facilitate lateral cross validation and high concurrency execution. This shift allowed the system to maintain a stable reasoning adherence of 89.2% while enabling A3 to process volumetric data without stalling downstream compliance and manufacturing logic.

sections.heading: Fragility and collapse prediction
paragraphs: Fragility curves quantify a structure seismic vulnerability by illustrating the probability of exceeding a given damage state at a specified ground motion intensity (Fig.  10 ). The deterministic baseline, which neglects microstructural variability, yields a smooth and narrow collapse probability curve, reaching a mean probability of approximately 72% at 2% drift. This narrowness provides a misleadingly high level of confidence because it fails to account for true system uncertainty. In contrast, the MEP posterior gives a more realistic and broader envelope, with a mean collapse probability of 80% at the same drift and a 95% upper bound approaching 100%. This broader distribution more accurately reflects the inherent uncertainty arising from microstructural heterogeneity. Fig. 10 Fragility curves: collapse probability versus drift (deterministic versus MEP posterior)

The primary limitation of deterministic models is their inability to represent tail risks. Rare but critical microstructural configurations, such as void clusters near the ITZ, can significantly reduce material toughness. Because deterministic models report only a single curve, they systematically underrepresent these low probability, high consequence events. The MEP corrects this by capturing a range of possible outcomes, but it can become computationally expensive when handling multiple layered structural elements due to the need for importance sampling to approximate posterior integrals.

An end-to-end workflow evaluation shows that the MAS completes a full design cycle, including 3D micro-CT segmentation, stochastic micromechanical convergence via the modified MEP, and manufacturing ready specification generation, in 30 min to 40 min per structural element. When microstructural descriptors are pre indexed, the inference driven (cached) workflow reduces to 7 min to 12 min, with no measurable degradation in predictive fidelity (bias increase below 0.5%). In contrast, equivalent finite element driven design iterations require 2–8 h of expert led modelling and engineering code compliance validation. This corresponds to an empirically observed reduction of approximately 75% in human intensive design cycles, while maintaining strict compliance with seismic safety constraints and preserving material structure consistency across all evaluated scenarios.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This work presents a production oriented multi-agent system (MAS) for the automated design and optimization of seismically resilient fiber reinforced concrete, validated across microstructural, material, and structural scales. The system demonstrates strong technical reliability, achieving 89.2% reasoning adherence, a mean predictive bias below 4% relative to high fidelity stochastic simulations, and a failure state classification F1 score of 0.98, while reducing human intensive design cycles by approximately 75% compared to conventional FEA based workflows.

At its core, the proposed framework establishes a tightly coupled, physics informed design pipeline that links microstructural characterization, stochastic homogenization, and structural performance prediction into a unified decision-making loop. The principal contribution of the Physical AI layer lies in the computationally efficient integration of a modified maximum entropy principle with stochastic micromechanical modelling of energy dissipation across FRC systems. This bidirectional coupling ensures that all design decisions remain consistent with both microstructural reality and structural performance requirements, enabling the generation of element specific FRC formulations that balance energy dissipation, strength, and constructability. The resulting framework represents a scalable and field deployable solution for automated, code compliant seismic FRC material design, extending beyond conventional workflows that treat material modelling, structural analysis, and engineering judgment as disjoint processes.

sections.heading: Future work and outlook
paragraphs: Although the MAS framework significantly reduces reliance on brute force simulations, its accuracy remains dependent on the quality of its training data and the calibration of its underlying models. The next frontier for this research is the integration of advanced PhysAI foundation models. Specifically, physics informed large language models and emerging large concept models (LCMs) hold the potential to embed fundamental physical laws, including fracture mechanics, interfacial transition zone scaling, and fiber pull out physics, directly into model inference and decision making.

Physics-informed LLMs trained on extensive micromechanical simulations and experimental datasets could learn to predict effective material properties while inherently embedding cyclic degradation laws. This would represent a significant advance beyond traditional methods such as the Mori–Tanaka scheme, which is limited by its assumptions of uniform strain and linear homogenization. Physics informed LLMs can also be trained to act as meta classifiers, combining MAS predictions with codified seismic design rules, for example drift ratios and ductility thresholds. LCMs can embed higher level structural concepts such as shear band formation or residual drift, enabling classification based not only on numerical patterns but also on mechanical meaning. This integration would mitigate wall specific misclassifications and enable the MAS to function as a knowledge rich, physics constrained seismic designer.

Such integration would drastically reduce model segmentation errors, accelerate the optimization loop, and extend the predictive power of the framework to unseen material systems. By evolving into next generation digital co design tools, MAS frameworks can empower engineers to create seismically resilient and sustainable concrete designs with unprecedented fidelity, adaptability, and efficiency, marking a significant step toward the full automation of material and structural design.
